The Java Spring Boot internship in short

In the SkillMe Java Spring Boot internship you build one of 3 projects, such as BankPulse: Enterprise Banking & Transaction Management System, a project where you build a simple banking app step by step, starting as a console program and ending as a small REST API backed by a real database. In week 1 you write a Java console program that can create bank accounts and record deposits and withdrawals in memory. By week 4 you harden your API with proper input validation, a global error handler, and automated tests, then document it with Swagger so anyone can explore it. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

Week by week

What each week of the Java Spring Boot internship covers

Shown for BankPulse: Enterprise Banking & Transaction Management System. The other projects follow the same four-week shape.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Accounts and Transactions in the Console

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Write a Java console program that can create bank accounts and record deposits and withdrawals in memory. This week is about getting comfortable with classes, objects and basic control flow before anything gets complicated.

    What you learn

    • Classes and objects with fields, constructors and methods
    • Using an ArrayList to store a collection of objects
    • Basic control flow with if/else and while loops
    • Reading user input with Scanner

    What you submit

    • Account and Bank classes with working deposit/withdraw logic
    • A Main class with a working console menu
    • A README with build/run instructions and a sample session
    • A short screenshot or terminal recording of a full session
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • You can open at least two accounts and see them both in the account list
    • Depositing and withdrawing valid amounts updates the balance correctly
    • Withdrawing more than the balance is rejected with a clear message, not an exception
    • The program runs from a menu loop until the user chooses Exit

    Stretch goal: Add a simple account type field (SAVINGS or CURRENT) that blocks withdrawals below a minimum balance for savings accounts.

  2. Week 2 of 4

    Transaction History and File Storage

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Add a transaction history to every account and save all data to a file so it survives between runs. This introduces you to composition between classes and basic file I/O, two skills every backend developer needs.

    What you learn

    • Composition: an Account holding a list of Transaction objects
    • Using enums for fixed categories like transaction type
    • Reading and writing plain text files with BufferedReader/BufferedWriter
    • Basic exception handling with try/catch

    What you submit

    • A Transaction class and an enum for transaction type
    • Accounts that keep and display their transaction history
    • A FileStorage class that saves and loads accounts from a text file
    • Data that survives closing and reopening the program
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • Every deposit and withdrawal appears in that account's statement in the right order
    • Closing and restarting the program keeps the accounts and their balances
    • Deleting or corrupting the data file does not crash the program on startup
    • The account list and statements still work correctly after the refactor

    Stretch goal: Add a transferFunds(fromAccount, toAccount, amount) method that records a withdrawal on one account and a deposit on the other as a single operation.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    Spring Boot REST API with H2

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Turn BankPulse into a real web service using Spring Boot, storing accounts in an in-memory H2 database with Spring Data JPA. This is your first REST API and your first taste of how most backend jobs actually work.

    What you learn

    • Setting up a Spring Boot project with Spring Web, Spring Data JPA and H2
    • Mapping a class to a database table with @Entity
    • Writing a JpaRepository and a @RestController with GET/POST endpoints
    • Returning proper HTTP status codes for success and error cases

    What you submit

    • A Spring Boot project with Account, Transaction entities and their repositories
    • REST endpoints for creating accounts, deposits, withdrawals and viewing history
    • Correct HTTP status codes for not-found and invalid-input cases
    • A short doc (or Postman collection) listing each endpoint with an example request
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • The app starts with mvn spring-boot:run and accounts persist in the H2 in-memory database
    • POST /accounts creates an account and GET /accounts lists it
    • Depositing and withdrawing through the API updates the balance and appends a transaction
    • Requesting a non-existent account id returns 404, not a stack trace
    • The H2 console shows the correct table structure and data

    Stretch goal: Add a POST /accounts/{id}/transfer endpoint that moves money between two accounts inside a single @Transactional method.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Validation, Tests and API Docs

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Harden your API with proper input validation, a global error handler, and automated tests, then document it with Swagger so anyone can explore it. This is the polish that turns a working demo into a project you can confidently show off.

    What you learn

    • Request validation with @Valid and Bean Validation annotations
    • A global exception handler with @ControllerAdvice
    • Writing service-layer tests with JUnit and Mockito
    • Documenting an API with springdoc-openapi (Swagger UI)

    What you submit

    • Validated request DTOs and a global exception handler
    • Swagger UI documenting every endpoint
    • At least 4 passing JUnit/Mockito tests for the service layer
    • A complete README with setup, run and test instructions
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • Sending an invalid amount (negative or missing) returns a clean 400 JSON error, not a stack trace
    • Requesting an account that does not exist returns a clean 404 JSON error
    • Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html lists and lets you try every endpoint
    • mvn test runs at least 4 tests and all of them pass
    • A new developer can set up and run the project using only the README

    Stretch goal: Add simple API key authentication using a request header, checked in a Spring filter before requests reach your controllers.

Is it for you?

Java Spring Boot internship: questions and answers

What will I build in this Spring Boot internship?

One of three apps (BankPulse, ShopSphere or TaskForge). Weeks 1 and 2 are core Java with file storage; week 3 turns it into a Spring Boot REST API with H2; week 4 adds validation, tests and API docs.

Do I need Spring Boot experience for the Java Spring Boot internship?

No. You need basic Java. Spring Boot is introduced in week 3, once the core Java version works.

What will I build in the Java Spring Boot internship?

You are assigned one of 3 projects: BankPulse: Enterprise Banking & Transaction Management System, ShopSphere: Multi-Tier E-Commerce & Inventory Hub or TaskForge: Personal Task & Habit Tracker. Each is a single project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the Java Spring Boot internship?

The Java Spring Boot internship works with Java 17, Spring Boot and Maven. Week 1: classes and objects with fields, constructors and methods; using an ArrayList to store a collection of objects. Week 2: composition: an Account holding a list of Transaction objects; using enums for fixed categories like transaction type. Week 3: setting up a Spring Boot project with Spring Web, Spring Data JPA and H2; mapping a class to a database table with @Entity. Week 4: request validation with @Valid and Bean Validation annotations; a global exception handler with @ControllerAdvice.

Do I need experience to apply for the Java Spring Boot internship?

You need the basics of Java 17, Spring Boot and Maven, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you write a Java console program that can create bank accounts and record deposits and withdrawals in memory. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each Java Spring Boot milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of BankPulse: Enterprise Banking & Transaction Management System, that means: you can open at least two accounts and see them both in the account list; depositing and withdrawing valid amounts updates the balance correctly; withdrawing more than the balance is rejected with a clear message, not an exception; the program runs from a menu loop until the user chooses Exit. Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the Java Spring Boot internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Built a Java console banking app with account creation, deposits and withdrawals; Modeled accounts and a bank using classes and an ArrayList; Added input validation so invalid withdrawals are rejected safely; Added transaction history tracking to my Java banking app using composition; Implemented file-based persistence so account data survives restarts; Handled file errors gracefully with try/catch instead of crashing; Rebuilt my Java banking app as a Spring Boot REST API with JPA and H2; Designed endpoints for accounts, deposits, withdrawals and transaction history; Learned to return proper HTTP status codes for not-found and invalid-input cases; Added request validation and a global error handler to my Spring Boot banking API; Wrote JUnit and Mockito tests for the account service layer; Documented the API with Swagger UI for easy exploration.

What are the other projects in the Java Spring Boot internship?

ShopSphere: Multi-Tier E-Commerce & Inventory Hub: Build a simple shop and inventory tool step by step, from a console app to a small REST API with orders and stock tracking. TaskForge: Personal Task & Habit Tracker: Build a task and habit tracking tool step by step, from a console app to a small REST API you can call from anywhere. Every project follows the same four-week shape, with one reviewed milestone a week.

Is the Java Spring Boot internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based: 8–10 interns are picked each month from those who complete the internship and hold an issued certificate. It is not paid to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
